4 The Frequentist Statistics Paradigm

4.1 Sampling, Inference and the Sample Mean

Terminology

  • •

    A population is the group of people or objects of interest. It is common to call the objects or people units or subjects.

  • •

    A sample is the subset of the population that is actually examined.

  • •

    There are many ways to choose the sample from the population:

    • –

      A simple random sample (SRS) of size n is a subset of size n of the population where each unit has the same chance of being included (and thus every possible subset of size n has equal probability of being selected).

    • –

      A stratified random sample is a sample composed by taking a SRS from each of several sub-groups (strata) which partition the population. For example, one could stratify by gender taking one random sample from men, another from women, and a third from non-binary.

    • –

      A quota sample is formed by sampling a given quota from each of the strata in the population. This is like stratified sampling, only the numbers taken from each strata are chosen to make the overall sample representative of the composition of the population, i.e. the same ratio of men:women:non-binary in the sample as in the population.

  • •

    Some common pitfalls involved in sampling:

    • –

      Is the sample truly random?

    • –

      Is the sample truly representative of the population?

    • –

      For surveys, is the wording of questions going to result in bias?

    • –

      For voluntarily completed questionnaires, will non-response lead to bias?

  • •

    A population parameter is some number that describes the population.

    • –

      e.g. the mean μ and variance σ2 (say, of a normal distribution)

    • –

      e.g. the proportion of successes p (for a binomial distribution)

  • •

    We will be most concerned with making inferences (learning) about such parameters.

  • •

    A statistic is a number that is calculated from the sample data, usually a summary.

    • –

      e.g. the sample mean X¯ and the sample variance s2.

    • –

      e.g. the sample proportion Y=p^.

  • •

    The sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic that describes how the statistic can vary from sample to sample.

    • –

      e.g. the distribution of X¯

    • –

      e.g. the distribution of Y

  • •

    Statistics are often used as estimators of population parameters.

    • –

      The sample proportion Y (also denoted by p^) is an estimator for the population proportion p.

  • •

    We will be concerned with two major aspects of estimators:

    • –

      whether or not they are biased - i.e. whether the centre of the sampling distribution and the actual distributions differ,

    • –

      their degree of variability - the more variable a statistic, the less useful it is as an estimator.

  • •

    Randomisation is the key weapon in ensuring zero bias.

  • •

    Variability is usually inversely proportional to sample size: the larger the sample, the less variable (more accurate) the estimators.

4.1.1 Inference

Inference is the act of drawing conclusions from certain basic facts and premisses.

  • •

    In classical frequentist statistics:

    • –

      The conclusions = what can we conclude about the population

    • –

      The basic facts = the sample data we see

    • –

      The premisses = the mathematical model that we believe describes the population (most of which we don’t see), the sample data, and the relationship between the sample and the population

  • •

    Inference is then the process of making statements about the population, given our mathematical model and the information we gained from our sample data.

  • •

    The inferences (conclusions) that we draw are rarely (if ever) certain, but are made with a degree of uncertainty.

  • •

    One of our aims will be to quantify uncertainty in our conclusions (in the Frequentist sense, via, for example, long-run coverage of confidence intervals or error rates of tests).

4.1.2 The Sample Mean X¯ as an Estimator for the Population Mean μ

Reminder: Sample Proportions are also Sample Means

Sample proportions from simple random samples, where each subject has 1 if the property is True and 0 if False, are just sample means. In the previous section, for example, p^ is the average voter value from the simple random sample (where 1 is a claim to vote for Trump, and a 0 is a claim not to).

  • •

    The sample mean, along with its properties, is the most used tool in the Frequentist statistical workshop, and most of our inferences will be based on sample means and standard deviations.

  • •

    We assume that:

    • –

      There is a population of interest, with mean value μ and standard deviation σ, often both unknown.

      • *

        Our main aim is to say something about μ.

      • *

        A secondary aim is to say something about σ.

      • *

        Ideally, we want to estimate μ with little or no bias and small variance, so that our guess is on target and can be expected to be close.

    • –

      We take a simple random sample of size n from this population (assumed sufficiently large to make successive samples (effectively) independent - see sampling without replacement approximation discussion in Section 3.2.2).

    • –

      We will label the sample values X1,X2,…⁢Xn.

    • –

      Before we see their values, each is a random variable having the same mean E⁢[Xi]=μ and standard deviation SD⁢[Xi]=σ as the population.

    • –

      We summarise that each Xi is independent and has the same distribution, expectation and variance by writing that X1,…,Xn are independent and identically distributed (iid) with mean μ and standard deviation σ.

  • •

    We now define the sample mean to be

    X¯=1n⁢∑i=1nXi.

Derivation of properties of the Sample Mean X¯

E⁢[X¯] = E⁢[1n⁢∑i=1nXi]=1n⁢E⁢[∑i=1nXi]=1n⁢∑i=1nE⁢[Xi] (60)
= 1n⁢∑i=1nμ=1n⁢n⁢μ=μ (61)
Var⁢[X¯] = Var⁢[1n⁢∑i=1nXi]=1n2⁢Var⁢[∑i=1nXi]=1n2⁢∑i=1nVar⁢[Xi] (62)
= 1n2⁢∑i=1nσ2=1n2⁢n⁢σ2=σ2n (63)
  • •

    So will the sample mean X¯ be a good estimator of the population mean μ?

  • •

    We know that the main properties of the random variable X¯ are:

    E⁢[X¯] =μ,
    Var⁢[X¯] =σ2/n, SD⁢[X¯] =σ/n
  • •

    We say that X¯ is an unbiased estimator of μ since E⁢[X¯]=μ. Again the expectation of the estimator is equal to the object that we are estimating!

  • •

    The Var⁢[X¯]=σ2/n is understood, and can be controlled via n, but it is not unbounded: it depends on the population variance σ2.

  • •

    Note that X¯ therefore has a smaller standard deviation than a single observation.

  • •

    Hence, the sample mean should yield quite accurate estimates of the population mean μ, and the larger the value of n the better. (See: The Weak Law of Large Numbers)

  • •

    If the main population of X is normally distributed with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then the distribution of the sample mean is also Normal, but now with X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n), irrespective of the size of n. This is because the sum of several normally distributed random variables is also normally distributed.

Discussion: The Sample Mean is a Random Variable, until it is Measured.

  • •

    Before we see the data, the sample mean is a random variable X¯; it can take many possible values, and has a probability distribution, an expectation, and a variance. This is similar to the X1,…,Xn themselves: they are each random variables, until they are measured.

  • •

    After we see the data, the individual X1,…,Xn become known numbers which we typically denote as x1,…,xn. The sample mean is now also just a number x¯, and is just one of the many possible outcomes we could have seen. See Figure 1 for further discussion.

  • •

    This echoes the Frequentist viewpoint that the only random aspect here is the sampling process (how we construct the SRS say), and all other things are fixed (even if they are unknown, like the population mean μ, for example). This somewhat limits what we can say probabilistically about, for example, the population mean, as we shall see when we discuss Confidence Intervals.

Example: Heights of US males

Question: Consider the distribution of heights of US males aged 18-74. The average height is about 69 inches, with standard deviation about 3 inches. Find the expectation and standard deviation of the sample mean from a SRS of size n=25 and n=50.

Solution: Suppose that we take a SRS of size n=25 heights and calculate its average. This should have expectation 69 and standard deviation 3/25=0.6 inches.

For a SRS of size n=50, this should also have expectation 69, but now a standard deviation 3/50=0.42 inches.

4.1.3 The Central Limit Theorem

  • •

    So, if the main population of X is normally distributed with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then the distribution of the sample mean is also Normal with
    X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n).

  • •

    However, what can we do if the population distribution (which is the distribution each of the Xi are drawn from) is not Normal?

  • •

    To answer this, we now discuss one of the most useful theorems ever created. It is, however, also one of the most overused.

Theorem: The Central Limit Theorem

Suppose X1, X2, …, Xn are n independent and identically distributed random variables, each with mean μ and variance σ2.

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that the distribution of the sample mean X¯=1n⁢∑iXi of these random variables is such that

X¯→N⁢(μ,σ2n)⁢ as ⁢n→∞,

regardless of the distribution of the Xi. The limit here is taken to mean it “converges in distribution”; see the Probability course for the precise definition.

  • •

    The approximation improves as n increases. An example of the sample distribution of sums of n independent exponential random variables is shown below, and illustrates this point.

  • •

    We typically say that the approximation is appropriate for n≥20, and perhaps satisfactory for n≥10. These values are rule-of-thumb; things get better as n increases as whether or not the approximation is reasonable will also depend on other features of the population distribution such as skewness, multi-modality, etc.

Prevalence of the Normal distribution

  • •

    The central limit theorem provides a plausible explanation for the fact that the distributions of many random variables studied in physical or psychological experiments are approximately Normal.

  • •

    A person’s height, for example, is influenced by many random factors (heredity, diet, etc.).

  • •

    These factors combine to give the person’s height – in an approximate sense these factors are “added”.

  • •

    As a result of the addition (sum, or mean) of many independent factors, we expect to see a Normal distribution of heights in a large number of people, and we do!

Example: Flaws in Carpets

Question:

  • •

    The number of flaws per square metre in a type of carpet is variable with mean 1.6 flaws per square metre and standard deviation 1.2 flaws per square metre.

  • •

    The distribution is not normal; in fact, it is discrete.

  • •

    An inspector studies 200 square metres of material, records the number of flaws found in each square metre, and calculates X¯, the mean number of flaws per square metre inspected.

  • •

    What is the probability that X¯ exceeds 1.7 per square metre?

Solution:

  • •

    Here we have a random sample X1,X2,…,X200, each with expectation E⁢[Xi]=1.6 and Var⁢[Xi]=1.22.

  • •

    By the central limit theorem, X¯∼N⁢(1.6,1.22/200)=N⁢(1.6,0.0852).

  • •

    We seek

    P⁢(X¯>1.7)=P⁢(X¯−μσ/n>1.7−μσ/n)=P⁢(Z>1.7−1.60.085)=P⁢(Z>1.18)

    (standardising random variables was covered in the Probability course).

  • •

    From tables, the probability that a standard normal random variable is less than or equal to 1.18 is 0.8810.

  • •

    Hence the probability that it exceeds 1.18 is 0.1190, and so the probability that X¯ will exceed 1.7 is also 0.1190.

4.1.4 Standard Errors and the t Distribution

The Standard Error of the Sample Mean

  • •

    This is all great: even if the individual Xi∼U⁢K⁢(μ,σ2) i.e. an UnKnown distribution with mean μ and variance σ2, the CLT tells us that the distribution of the sample mean is X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n) as n→∞. However, note that we need to know the population variance σ2 in order to use these results, which often we don’t know.

  • •

    What if the population sd σ is unknown, and n is large?

    • –

      Estimate the population standard deviation σ by the sample standard deviation, which before the data is measured is the random variable S:

      S=1n−1⁢∑i=1n(Xi−X¯)2=1n−1⁢(∑i=1nXi2−n⁢X¯2) (64)

      and after the data is measured becomes just the real number s:

      s=1n−1⁢∑i=1n(xi−x¯)2=1n−1⁢(∑i=1nxi2−n⁢x¯2) (65)
  • •

    For i.i.d. observations, E⁢[S2]=σ2, and is hence an unbiased estimator, so we can expect the estimate to be reasonably good.

  • •

    For large n, S will also be close to σ, hence s is a reasonable estimate for σ and we can estimate the standard deviation of the sample mean σ/n by the standard error of the sample mean, s/n.

  • •

    In addition, if we insert (rather casually33 3 for those interested, using Slutsky’s theorem) this standard error, in random variable form S/n, into the Central Limit Theorem, we get the result:

    X¯−μS/n∼N⁢(0,1) if n is sufficiently large
  • •

    However, if n is not sufficiently large then

    • –

      s is a poor estimate for σ

    • –

      X¯−μS/n is no longer Normally distributed

  • •

    In general, we need n≥30 for these results to hold (again this value of n is a rule-of-thumb, and will depend on other features of the population distribution, e.g. skewness, multi-modality, etc.).

The t Distribution

  • •

    What if the population sd σ is unknown, and n is small?

  • •

    As discussed above, if n is small, then s is a poor estimate for σ, hence X¯−μS/n is no longer normally distributed, hence we can’t make nice distributional statements such as those given above.

  • •

    The exception to this is if the distribution of the Xi themselves is Normal (or even approximately Normal) then we can proceed as follows.

  • •

    We still estimate σ by s, but now we use the t distribution instead of the Normal distribution.

  • •

    The sample mean then has the following distribution

    X¯−μS/n∼tn−1

    and our sampling theory still holds, albeit replacing a standard Normal distribution for a t-distribution.

Definition: The t distribution

A random variable T has a t distribution with degrees of freedom parameter ν if it has continuous distribution with p.d.f.

f⁢(t|ν)=Γ⁢(ν+12)ν⁢π⁢Γ⁢(ν2)⁢(1+t2ν)−ν+12 (66)

where the normalising factor employs the gamma function Γ, a continuous version of the factorial function, with Γ⁢(n)=(n−1)! for positive integer n.

  • •

    We write that T∼tν, and note that E⁢[T]=0 and Var⁢[T]=ν/(ν−2) for ν>2, (∞ or undefined otherwise).

  • •

    Calculating directly using f⁢(t|ν) is difficult, so we use pre-calculated tables, just as for the Normal distribution.

  • •

    The full definition of the Gamma function is

    Γ⁢(z)=∫0∞xz−1⁢e−x⁢𝑑x (67)

    but this is not particularly useful for our purposes. More concise expressions exist for the half integer values of z that are needed in equation (66).

Discussion: Why do we need the t-distribution? [non-examinable]

  • •

    Given μ and σ, we have that X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n) and equivalently we can write Z=(X¯−μ)/(σ/n)∼N⁢(0,1).

  • •

    When σ is unknown we need to estimate it by the sample sd, s.

  • •

    However, like the sample mean X¯, until we see the data the sample sd is also a random variable S.

  • •

    So now T=(X¯−μ)/(S/n) is a random variable, the expression for which itself involves two other random variables (X¯ and S).

  • •

    When the population is (approximately) normally distributed, X¯ and S2 are independent, and W2=(n−1)⁢S2/σ2∼χn−12, that is, a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom.

  • •

    So we have that:

    T=X¯−μS/n=(X¯−μ)/(σ/n)((n−1)⁢S2/σ2)/(n−1)=ZW2/(n−1)
  • •

    It turns out that such a rv, i.e. composed of an independent standard normal rv and chi-square rv with ν df as above, yields a t distribution also with ν df, i.e. T=Z/W2/(n−1)∼tn−1.

Properties of the t Distribution

  • •

    The tn−1 distribution has a similar shape to a standard normal N⁢(0,1).

  • •

    The tn−1 has “fatter tails” – more probability is assigned to values farther from the centre and with the tails getting fatter as n gets smaller.

  • •

    The tn−1 has variance >1, and is given by n−1n−3 for n≥4 and ∞ otherwise (note here we are using ν=n−1). It has greater spread than a standard normal random variable.

  • •

    limn→∞tn−1=N⁢(0,1), so it converges towards the normal distribution as n gets larger.

  • •

    Like the Normal, we need to use tables (or a computer) to find probabilities.

  • •

    Recall that use of the tn−1 distribution here requires the original population to be (approximately) normally distributed. We can test whether our data are normally distributed via a normal quantile plot (easier to assess for larger values of n (say, greater that 15)).

Example: Lightbulbs

  • •

    A light bulb manufacturer claims that the mean life of a lightbulb is 1200 hours.

  • •

    A consumer association randomly selects 16 bulbs, with the intention of rejecting the manufacturers claim if the sample mean X¯ is less than 1160 hours.

  • •

    The sample standard deviation is s=200

  • •

    Question 1: Assuming such lightbulb lifetimes are normally distributed, what is the probability that the manufacturers will be declared dishonest if, in fact, they are honest?

  • •

    Question 2: Find a value c so that the probability that the lightbulb sample mean is smaller than c is 0.05.

  1. 1.
    • •

      If the population distribution (i.e. lightbulb lifetimes) is exactly normal, then we have that (with n=16):

      T=X¯−μS/16∼t15 (68)

      Note that T is a random variable (before data are observed) - any hypothetical sample of n=16 bulbs would yield different values for the two estimator random variables (X¯ and S) that are present in the expression for T. If the population distribution (i.e. lightbulb lifetimes) is approximately normal, then the distributional statement (68) holds approximately.

    • •

      Whether distributional statement (68) holds exactly or approximately, we want to make probabilistic statements about the sample mean estimator X¯ alone (as opposed to T, say, which also involves S). For our purposes, we will do this by casually replacing the random variable S with our sample estimate s, and make the further approximation that:

      T=X¯−μ200/16∼t15
    • •

      Now, if the manufacturers are honest, then μ=1200, and the probability that this (unobserved) sample mean X¯ is smaller than 1160 is

      P⁢(X¯<1160) = P⁢(X¯−1200200/16<1160−1200200/16)
      = P⁢(T<−0.8),T∼t15
      = P⁢(T>0.8),by⁢symmetry
    • •

      Examining tables of the t distribution with 15 df, we see that P⁢(T>0.691)=0.25 and P⁢(T>0.866)=0.20, so the probability we require is somewhere between 0.20 and 0.25 (can use linear interpolation here to improve this).

  2. 2.
    • •

      The t distribution is most often used in reverse, as follows.

    • •

      We wish to find a value c so that the probability that the lightbulb sample mean is smaller than c is 0.05, ie. P⁢(X¯<c)=0.05.

    • •

      For 15df, the t table shows us that P⁢(T<−1.753)=P⁢(T>1.753)=0.05.

    • •

      Therefore, it must be the case that P⁢(X¯−1200200/16<−1.753)=0.05.

    • •

      Rearranging inside the probability shows us that:
      P⁢(X¯<1200−(50)⁢(1.753))=0.05, i.e. P⁢(X¯<1112.35)=0.05.

    • •

      Thus, if the consumer association want to accuse the manufacturers of dishonesty with probability 5% of being wrong, their threshold under these circumstances should be 1112.35. We will formalise this argument soon.

4.2 Confidence Intervals

4.2.1 Inference about μ

  • •

    Suppose we will take a simple random sample X1,…,Xn from a population with mean μ and variance σ2.

  • •

    We know (CLT) that the sample mean is approximately

    X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2n)

    for sufficiently large n.

  • •

    Since we know the distribution of X¯, we can make statements of probability about where the random variable (rv) X¯ is likely to be.

  • •

    For example, we can determine from Normal tables that

    P⁢(−1.96≤X¯−μσ/n≤1.96)=0.95
  • •

    So given μ and σ2, we can make an inference about X¯.

  • •

    But we’re really interested in μ, not X¯.

  • •

    We can rearrange the previous probability statement about X¯ into

    P⁢(X¯−1.96⁢σn≤μ≤X¯+1.96⁢σn)=0.95.
  • •

    This says that μ lies in the interval [X¯−1.96⁢σn,X¯+1.96⁢σn] with probability 0.95, however…

  • •

    Important: This is a random interval – the probability is with respect to the random variable X¯ before data are observed (and hence don’t know). We therefore can’t use such probabilistic statements to make inference about μ (which is fixed, but unknown).

4.2.2 Confidence Intervals: Definition

  • •

    Suppose we observe a particular sample X1=x1,…,Xn=xn and calculate X¯=x¯.

  • •

    We can now substitute our observed x¯ for the random variable X¯ into our random interval to construct a confidence interval (CI) for μ

    [x¯−1.96⁢σn,x¯+1.96⁢σn]
  • •

    We call this a 95% confidence interval as the theoretical probability statement from which the confidence interval was obtained had probability 0.95 (i.e. the statement above involving the random variable X¯ before the data was observed).

Important!

  • •

    A Confidence Interval is not a probability statement. Our confidence interval is a realisation of the random interval – in the same way x¯ is a realisation of X¯

  • •

    Once it is observed, it is no longer random.

  • •

    There is no uncertainty (probability) associated with the CI and only one of two cases can occur

    • –

      The interval contains μ,

    • –

      The interval does not contain μ – i.e. this particular sample gave an x¯ which was not close to the true mean μ.

  • •

    Instead, if we took many samples and calculated a sample mean and a 95% confidence interval for each sample, then 95% of the intervals should contain μ.

  • •

    As an example, Figure 2 shows 100 Confidence intervals for population mean μ constructed from 100 samples, each of size 10, taken from a N(0,1) population.

Beware!

  • •

    μ is not a random variable; it is fixed, but unknown.

  • •

    A confidence interval is not a probability statement, nor is it a random interval. It is a realisation of a random interval.

  • •

    Be careful not to write (or even think)

    P⁢(x¯−1.96⁢σn≤μ≤x¯+1.96⁢σn)=0.95

    This has no meaning – to have a probability we must be considering something random! (At least, in the Frequentist Paradigm.)

  • •

    If we were to take many samples then 95% of the time μ would be inside the 95% confidence interval.

General Confidence Intervals

  • •

    We aren’t restricted to finding confidence intervals for only the mean.

  • •

    Given a random sample X¯=(X1,X2,…,Xn) and two statistics [u⁢(X¯),v⁢(X¯)]

  • •

    Then a realisation [u⁢(x¯),v⁢(x¯)] of the random interval [u⁢(X¯),v⁢(X¯)] is called

    • –

      a confidence interval

    • –

      at confidence level (1−α)

    • –

      for a population parameter θ

    whenever

    P⁢(u⁢(X¯)≤θ≤v⁢(X¯))= 1−α
  • •

    In general, a (1−α)% confidence interval for an unknown parameter θ is a range between two numbers such that the method of producing the interval gives an interval which contains the true value of θ, (1−α)% of the time.

4.2.3 Confidence Intervals for the Population Mean

σ known

  • •

    Suppose that

    • –

      We have a simple random sample X1,X2,…,Xn

    • –

      The population standard deviation σ is known

    • –

      Either

      • *

        We know the population is Normal

      • *

        OR n is large (≥20 say, so we can safely use the CLT)

    • –

      We calculated the observed sample mean x¯

  • •

    Then a (1−α)% confidence interval for μ is

    x¯±z∗⁢σn

    where z∗ is called a critical value of a standard Normal random variable and is such that

    P⁢(−z∗≤Z≤z∗)=1−α

For example, α=0.05 gives z∗=1.96 from the Normal Table, as was used above.

Example: Candle Lifetimes

Question:

  • •

    A candle making process is known to produce candles whose lifetime have a variance of 0.4 hours squared.

  • •

    The average lifetime is unknown.

  • •

    The lifetimes of a random sample of six candles are:

    8.1,8.7,9.2,7.8,8.4,9.4

    hours respectively.

  • •

    The lifetime is known to be Normally distributed.

  • •

    Find a 99% confidence interval for the population mean.

Solution:

  • •

    Sample statistics are x¯=8.6, n=6.

  • •

    σ is known and the lifetimes are normally distributed ⟹ X¯∼N⁢(μ,σ2/n).

  • •

    99% CI implies α=0.01. The critical value z∗ with α/2=0.5% of the area to the right of z∗ on a standard Normal curve is z∗=2.575.

  • •

    So a 99% CI for μ is

    x¯±z∗⁢σn = 8.6±2.575×0.46
    = 8.6±0.66
    =[7.94,9.26]

σ unknown, n small, Normal

  • •

    Suppose that

    • –

      We have a simple random sample X1,X2,…,Xn

    • –

      The population standard deviation σ is unknown

    • –

      We know the population is Normal

    • –

      n is small

    • –

      We calculated the observed sample mean x¯, and the observed sample standard deviation s

  • •

    Then a (1−α)% confidence interval for μ is (using the same argument as above):

    x¯±tn−1∗⁢sn

    where tn−1∗ is the critical value of a t distributed random variable with (n−1) degrees of freedom such that

    P⁢(−tn−1∗≤T≤tn−1∗)=1−α.

For example, we see that α=0.05 and n=11 gives t10∗=2.228 from the t-table.

Example: Iron Retention in Mice

Question:

  • •

    An experiment was performed to determine how well a particular form of iron (Fe3+) is retained in the body.

  • •

    The investigators gave Fe3+ to 18 mice.

  • •

    The percentage of iron retained is listed for each mouse below.

    Fe3+ 2.20 2.93 3.08 3.49 4.11 4.95 5.16 5.54 5.68
    6.25 7.25 7.90 8.85 11.96 15.54 15.89 18.30 18.59
  • •

    x¯=8.20 and s=5.45

  • •

    Obtain a 90% confidence interval for the population mean for the Fe3+ data

Solution:

  • •

    σ is unknown, so first check for Normality of the data: draw a Boxplot and a Normal Quantile Plot.

Boxplots

We draw a boxplot by: (a) Drawing a box with lower boundary at Q⁢1 (the first quartile, such that 25% of data are less than this value) and upper boundary Q⁢3 (the third quartile, such that 75% of data are less than this value), (b) draw a line inside the box at Q⁢2 (the median: 50% data less than this). (c) Mark outliers, if any, as individual crosses. Outliers are any values larger than Q⁢3+(1.5)⁢I⁢Q⁢R, or any values smaller than Q⁢1−(1.5)⁢I⁢Q⁢R, where the InterQuartile Range, I⁢Q⁢R=Q⁢3−Q⁢1. (d) Excluding the outliers, draw lines from the new minimum value (if any) up to the box, and from the new maximum value (if any) down to the box. These lines are called the “whiskers”.

Example: Iron Retention in Mice

We have n=18 and so the median Q⁢2 is the midpoint of the 9th and 10th data points so Q⁢2=(5.68+6.25)/2=5.965, Q⁢1 is at the 5th data point so Q⁢1=4.11 and similarly Q⁢3 is at the 14th data point so Q⁢3=11.96. Therefore I⁢Q⁢R=Q⁢3−Q⁢1=11.96−4.11=7.85. As Q⁢3+(1.5)⁢I⁢Q⁢R is larger than all the data and as Q⁢1−(1.5)⁢I⁢Q⁢R is smaller than all the data, there are no outliers. See boxplot on next page.

Normal Quantile Plots

We draw a Normal quantile plot by a) ordering the n data values x1,…,xn from smallest to largest, b) plotting these ordered values against the n quantiles zk that satisfy Φ⁢(zk)=kn+1,k=1,…,n, where Φ⁢(x) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard Normal distribution (i.e. mean 0, variance 1), that we get from the Normal table. If the plotted points form roughly a straight line, then we conclude that there is no evidence against normality.

Example: Iron Retention in Mice

We have n=18 and the largest data value is 18.59 which we plot against z18 which satisfies Φ⁢(z18)=1818+1≃0.947. From the Normal table we see that z18≃1.62 and we hence plot the point with coordinates (1.62, 18.59). Doing this for all ordered points (starting with the largest and working down is easiest!) gives the following table, and quantile plot:

k 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9
Ordered data xk 2.2 2.93 3.08 3.49 4.11 4.95 5.16 5.54 5.68
Φ⁢(zk)=kn+1 0.0526 0.105 0.158 0.211 0.263 0.316 0.368 0.421 0.474
Quantiles zk -1.62 -1.25 -1.00 -0.80 -0.63 -0.48 -0.34 -0.20 -0.07
k 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 17 18
Ordered data xk 6.25 7.25 7.9 8.85 11.96 15.54 15.89 18.3 18.59
Φ⁢(zk)=kn+1 0.526 0.579 0.632 0.684 0.737 0.789 0.842 0.895 0.947
Quantiles zk 0.07 0.20 0.34 0.48 0.63 0.80 1.00 1.25 1.62

(See solution to Q15 on the Problems Sheets for a further example).

  • •

    Normal Quantile plot is curved: not approximately a straight line, boxplot skew: Data don’t look Normal!

  • •

    Sample size is only 18, so CLT plus direct estimate of σ by s does not apply.

  • •

    Can’t really do anything with the theory and methods we have – a nonparametric technique may help (see second year course).

  • •

    Alternatively, we could consider taking logs of our data.

Example: Iron Retention in Mice (Logs)

  • •

    The log of the percentage of iron retained is listed for each mouse below.

    Log(Fe3+) 0.79 1.08 1.12 1.25 1.41 1.60 1.64 1.71 1.74
    1.83 1.98 2.07 2.18 2.48 2.74 2.77 2.91 2.92
  • •

    x¯=1.90 and s=0.66

  • •

    Question: Can we obtain a 90% confidence interval for the population mean of the log iron retention.

  • •

    σ is still unknown, check for Normality of the log(data)

  • •

    Normal Quantile plot is roughly a straight line, therefore we have approximate Normality now.

  • •

    n small, data appear normal ⟹ we can construct a CI using t-distribution, so we have: x¯±tn−1∗⁢sn

  • •

    We want a 90% CI, so find the critical value from t tables with α=0.1.

  • •

    t17∗=1.740 (from t17 table with 5% probability to right of t17∗).

  • •

    So the CI is x¯±tn−1∗⁢sn= 1.90±1.740×0.66/18=[1.63,2.17]

σ unknown, n large

  • •

    Suppose that

    • –

      We have a simple random sample X1,X2,…,Xn

    • –

      The population standard deviation σ is unknown

    • –

      The sample is large, n≥30

    • –

      We calculated the observed sample mean x¯, and the observed sample standard deviation s

  • •

    Then a (1−α)% confidence interval for μ is

    x¯±z∗⁢sn

    where z∗ is the critical value of the standard normal random variable such that

    P⁢(−z∗≤Z≤z∗)=1−α

Example: Cuckoo Eggs

  • •

    A sample of 100 cuckoo eggs was obtained. The lengths in millimetres of the eggs were as follows.

    22.5 20.1 23.3 22.9 23.1 22.0 22.3 23.6 24.7 23.7
    24.0 20.4 21.3 22.0 24.2 21.7 21.0 20.1 21.9 21.9
    21.7 22.6 20.9 21.6 22.2 22.5 22.2 24.3 22.3 22.6
    20.1 22.0 22.8 22.0 22.4 22.3 20.6 22.1 21.9 23.0
    22.0 22.0 22.1 22.0 19.6 22.8 22.0 23.4 23.8 23.3
    22.5 22.3 21.9 22.0 21.7 23.3 22.2 22.3 22.8 22.9
    23.7 22.0 21.9 22.2 24.4 22.7 23.3 24.0 23.6 22.1
    21.8 21.1 23.4 23.8 23.3 24.0 23.5 23.2 24.0 22.4
    23.9 22.0 23.9 20.9 23.8 25.0 24.0 21.7 23.8 22.8
    23.1 23.1 23.5 23.0 23.0 21.8 23.0 23.3 22.4 22.4
  • •

    x¯=22.57, s=1.07

  • •

    Obtain a 95% confidence interval for the population mean egg length.

  • •

    egg length 95% CI?

  • •

    n=100 is large, therefore s should be decent estimate for σ, therefore use normal approximation.

  • •

    Therefore our CI has the form: x¯±z∗⁢sn

  • •

    Check the plots just in case – look approximately normal, slight skew as quartiles are not equidistant from median. If there were outliers here they may affect the estimate for σ.

  • •

    95% CI ⇒ we need the critical value z∗=1.96 (from normal table at 0.975).

  • •

    x¯±z∗⁢sn= 22.57±1.96×1.07/100=[22.36,22.78]

Summary

  • •

    We have seen the following cases:

    • –

      σ is known

      • *

        n is large, or population is Normal

        x¯±z∗⁢σn
    • –

      σ is unknown

      • *

        n is small and the population is Normal

        x¯±tn−1∗⁢sn
      • *

        n is large

        x¯±z∗⁢sn
  • •

    If we don’t find ourselves in any of these cases, then we need to use alternative methods (e.g. nonparametric methods).

4.2.4 Margin of Error

  • •

    Most of our confidence intervals have the form

    x¯ ±cn
    Estimate ±Margin of error
  • •

    The value of the margin of error is an indication of the inaccuracy of the estimate at this level of confidence.

  • •

    The larger the value of n, the smaller the margin of error.

  • •

    As we have seen earlier, we can choose a particular sample size in order to guarantee a certain margin of error.

Example: Margin of Error for Candle Data

  • •

    The candle data: we know that σ=0.4

  • •

    Hence the margin of error for a 95% CI would be

    1.96⁢0.4n
  • •

    Suppose we want to find n such that the margin of error is ±0.1.

    1.96⁢0.4n =0.1
    1.96⁢0.40.1 =n
    153.7 =n
  • •

    Hence we need a sample of about 154 candles to give a 95% CI with a margin of error of ±0.1

4.2.5 Warnings

  • •

    The theory behind confidence intervals comes with a lot of assumptions.

  • •

    Particularly, the theory applies to taking simple random samples from a large population.

  • •

    The sample mean X¯ is strongly affected by outliers and skewness – this can heavily impact the reliability of the CI.

  • •

    Strong assumptions of Normality are often made (in fact, far too often in many supposedly scientific areas), sometimes inappropriately e.g. when n is small. Always check the data for Normality.

4.3 Hypothesis Testing

4.3.1 Introduction

  • •

    We are now in a position to answer scientific statements about the real world.

  • •

    With the cuckoo egg data, we found that a 95% CI for the mean length μ of cuckoo eggs was [22.36,22.78].

  • •

    One way to test a hypothesis about the value of μ is to construct a CI for μ.

  • •

    If the hypothesised value is contained within the confidence interval, the data support the hypothesis, otherwise, the data do not support the hypothesis.

Terminology

  • •

    Suppose we are interested in a single unknown population parameter θ – e.g. the mean μ of a population, or the population sd σ.

  • •

    Suppose also that we have a number r which we either believe may be the value for θ, or is a possible value for θ against which we wish to compare.

Definition: Null and Alternative Hypotheses

  • •

    We construct two hypotheses:

    • –

      H0 is the null hypothesis – H0 generally hypothesises that θ is equal to some value r.

    • –

      Ha is the alternative hypothesis – Ha denies the null hypothesis. The type of denial determines whether it is a one- or two-sided test.

  • •

    A two-sided hypothesis test is stated as

    H0: θ=r
    Ha: θ≠r
  • •

    The one-sided hypothesis test is stated as

    Either ⁢H0: θ=r Or ⁢H0: θ=r
    Ha: θ<r Ha: θ>r

Big Question

Given a particular sample, should we reject the null hypothesis or not?

Note:

  • •

    Choosing a one- or two-sided test is a matter of judgement.

  • •

    We will mostly be concerned with two-sided tests.

Reminder

We have seen already many cases where X¯ is an estimator for μ, a population mean, and S⁢E⁢(X¯)=s/n is its standard error. From such considerations we have already constructed confidence intervals using Normal and t distibutions.

Examples of Hypotheses

Question: For each of the following cases, write down appropriate null and alternative hypotheses, and state whether it is a one- or two- sided test.

  • •

    Let μ be the mean of the population of cuckoo egg lengths. An ornithologist wishes to test the hypothesis that μ=22.5.

  • •

    A lightbulb manufacturer claims that the average lifetime of its lightbulbs is guaranteed to be at least 1200 hours. A consumer association wishes to test this claim.

  • •

    Are the variances in two populations, σ12 and σ22, the same or different?

  • •

    Simple linear regression equations are of the form Y=a+b⁢X, where we usually estimate a and b from the data. Is the regression on X of any use for predicting Y?

Solution:

  • •

    Ornithologist: two-sided test

    H0:

    μ=22.5

    Ha:

    μ≠22.5.

  • •

    Lightbulbs: one-sided test

    H0:

    μ=1200 hours

    Ha:

    μ<1200 hours.

  • •

    Variances: two-sided test

    H0:

    σ12=σ22

    Ha:

    σ12≠σ22

  • •

    Regression: test whether slope b is equal to zero or not (two-sided test)

    H0:

    b=0

    Ha:

    b≠0

4.3.2 Hypothesis Testing via Confidence Intervals

Method: Two-sided case

If we have:

  • •

    A two-sided hypothesis, H0:θ=r, Ha:θ≠r.

  • •

    An estimator for θ.

  • •

    The sampling distribution of the estimator (as a function of θ).

  • •

    A level of significance α.

Then we can construct a 1−α confidence interval for θ, and then there is

  • •

    Evidence to reject H0 if r lies outside the confidence interval, and find the test statistically significant at the α% level of significance.

  • •

    No evidence to reject (i.e. fail to reject) H0 otherwise and find the test not significant at the α% level of significance.

Method: One-sided case

If we have:

  • •

    A one-sided hypothesis, H0:θ=r, Ha:θ<r (or Ha:θ>r).

  • •

    An estimator for θ.

  • •

    The sampling distribution of the estimator (as a function of θ).

  • •

    A level of significance α.

Then we can construct a 1−2⁢α confidence interval for θ, and there is

  • •

    Evidence to reject H0 if r falls to the right (left) of the confidence interval.

  • •

    No evidence to reject (i.e. fail to reject) H0 otherwise.

Example: Candle Lifetimes

Question:

  • •

    For the earlier example of candle lifetimes, let H0:μ=9.2 and Ha:μ≠9.2. Should we reject H0 or not, at the 1% significance level?

Solution:

  • •

    Significance level α= 1% → 1−α=99% confidence interval

  • •

    As previously seen in Section 4.2, with n small, normally distributed, σ known, a CI was given by

    x¯±z∗⁢σn=  8.6±2.575×0.46=[7.94,9.26]
  • •

    99% CI contains μ=9.2 therefore there is:

    “no evidence to reject H0 at the 1% significance level”.

Example: Chocolate Bars

  • •

    Six randomly selected chocolate bars weigh

    103, 101, 97, 95, 101, 98

    grams with x¯=99.17, s=2.99.

  • •

    Test the hypothesis that the mean weight μ of all such chocolate bars is 100g.

  • •

    Let’s choose significance level α=5%.

  • •

    Two sided test: H0:μ=100⁢g, Ha:μ≠100⁢g.

  • •

    Boxplot and quantile plot: data looks fairly normal.

  • •

    σ unknown, n small, data normal therefore use t distribution. 95% CI is

    x¯±t5,0.975∗⁢sn= 99.17±2.571⁢2.996=[96.03,102.31]
  • •

    95% CI contains μ=100 which implies test not significant at 5% level, and therefore we:

    “fail to reject H0 at the 5% significance level”.

Example: Nicotine, two sided test

  • •

    To test whether the mean nicotine content of a brand of cigarettes is the advertised value of 1.4mg, a health group takes a random sample of n=80 cigarettes, with x¯=1.5, s=0.3.

  • •

    Consider a two sided test H0:μ=1.4, Ha:μ≠1.4. Would they reject H0 at the 10% significance level, or not?

  • •

    n large ⟹ normal approximation, σ≃s, and the 90% CI for μ is

    x¯±z∗⁢sn= 1.5±1.645⁢0.380=[1.44,1.56]

    does not contain μ=1.4 therefore there is:

    “evidence to reject H0 at 10% level of significance”.

Example: Nicotine, one sided test

  • •

    Same nicotine example as above, but consider a one sided test:

    H0:μ=1.4, Ha:μ>1.4.

  • •

    Would they reject H0 at the 5% significance level, or not?

  • •

    one sided test at α=5% level requires a 1−2⁢α= 90% confidence interval, which we already calculated above! This was found to be [1.44,1.56].

  • •

    μ=1.4 is to the left of the CI so therefore there is:

    “evidence to reject H0 at the 5% level of significance”.

Example: Nicotine, one sided test (the other side)

  • •

    Same as above, but consider a one sided test

    H0:μ=1.4, Ha:μ<1.4.

  • •

    Would they reject H0 at the 5% significance level, or not?

  • •

    A one sided test at α=5% level requires the same 1−2⁢α= 90% confidence interval as before which was [1.44,1.56].

  • •

    μ=1.4 is not to the right of the 90% CI therefore we

    “fail to reject H0 at the 5% level of significance”.

4.3.3 Hypothesis Testing via p-Values

Method

Definition: p-value

  • •

    Calculating CIs is one way to test a hypothesis – an alternative is to calculate an appropriate test statistic from the data.

  • •

    We can then work out the probability of observing a value at least as extreme as the statistic under the assumption that H0 is true.

  • •

    This probability is known as the p-value.

  • •

    We find the p-value by comparing the value of the statistic with critical values of the relevant sampling distribution.

  • •

    The more extreme the statistic, the more unlikely it is that the assumptions of H0 are true.

    small p-value ⟹ reject H0

    (the test statistic is sufficiently extreme that it is unlikely to have occurred under H0)

  • •

    The threshold for p-value = level of significance α.

  • •

    A typical test statistic, for testing the population mean, is of course the (standardized) sample mean.

Note

  • •

    Finding the p-value is like finding the confidence of a confidence interval which has one boundary on the test statistic.

  • •

    For a one-tailed test, the p-value is the tail probability corresponding to being “at least as extreme” as the value of our test statistic.

  • •

    For a two-tailed test, we have to remember we have two tails to count as we can be “at least as extreme” in two directions, so the p-value will be double that of a one-tailed test.

Example: Candle lifetimes: p-value

  • •

    Again, for the earlier example of candle lifetimes, let H0:μ=9.2 and Ha:μ≠9.2. Find the p-value. Should we reject H0 or not?

  • •

    Again, n small, normally distributed, σ known.

  • •

    Under H0, i.e. assuming H0 is true, μ=9.2, so X¯∼N⁢(9.2,0.4/6)

    p-value =probability of observing X¯ at least as extreme as x¯=8.6, given H0
    =P⁢(X¯≤8.6)+P⁢(X¯≥9.8)(9.8=9.2+(9.2−8.6))
    =2⁢P⁢(X¯≥9.8) (by symmetry about μ=9.2)
    =2⁢P⁢(X¯−9.20.4/6≥9.8−9.20.4/6)(using μ=9.2 given H0)
    =2⁢P⁢(Z≥9.8−9.20.4/6)(withZ∼N⁢(0,1))
    =2⁢P⁢(Z≥2.32)
    =2⁢(1−P⁢(Z≤2.32))
    =2⁢(1−0.9898)=0.0204
  • •

    Therefore, as the p-value < 0.05, we reject H0 at the 5% significance level.

  • •

    But we would fail to reject H0 at the 1% significance level.

Example: Chocolate bar: p-value

  • •

    For the chocolate bar example, we had H0:μ=100⁢g and Ha:μ≠100⁢g. Give a lower bound on the p-value. Should we reject H0 or not?

  • •

    Remember we had n=6, x¯=99.17 and s=2.99.

  • •

    Now, under H0, we have

    X¯−100S/n∼t5
    p-value =probability of observing X¯ at least as extreme as x¯=99.17, given H0
    =P⁢(X¯<99.17)+P⁢(X¯>100.83)
    =2⁢P⁢(X¯>100.83) (by symmetry about μ=100)
    =2⁢P⁢(T>100.83−1002.99/6)(with ⁢T∼t5)
    =2⁢P⁢(T>0.68)
  • •

    From t5 table the first value is P⁢(T>0.727)=0.25. Since 0.68<0.727, we know P⁢(T>0.68)>0.25, so the p-value must be at least 2×0.25=0.5 (large!)

  • •

    Hence, there is no evidence to reject H0 for any reasonable significance value.

Example: Nicotine: p-value

  • •

    For the nicotine example, calculate the p-value for the one sided test given by H0:μ=1.4, Ha:μ>1.4.

  • •

    Remember we had: n=80 cigarettes, with x¯=1.5, s=0.3.

  • •

    One sided test: extremity means only to the right of 1.4!

    p-value =probability of observing X¯ at least as extreme as x¯=1.5, given H0
    =P⁢(X¯>1.5)
    =P⁢(Z>1.5−1.40.3/80) (standardize as usual, using μ=1.4)
    =P⁢(Z>2.98)
    =0.0014⁢ (tables)
  • •

    test is significant at the 0.14% level.

  • •

    This is a very low p-value! Evidence to reject H0 at all reasonable significance levels!

  • •

    Note: p-value for two sided test is of course simply

    P⁢(X¯<1.3)+P⁢(X¯>1.5)=0.0028
  • •

    The two sided test is significant at the 0.28% level.

4.3.4 Case Summary

H0:μ=μ0Ha:μ≠μ0

σ n sampling confidence test statistic
interval for p-value
known small normal x¯±z∗⁢σn X¯−μ0σ/n∼N⁢(0,1)
known large any x¯±z∗⁢σn X¯−μ0σ/n∼N⁢(0,1)
unknown small normal x¯±tn−1∗⁢sn X¯−μ0S/n∼tn−1

For the cases not listed in the table above, we would need to enlist the use of non-parametric hypothesis tests (not covered in this course).

4.3.5 Terminology Summary

observed standardised observed standardised
sample mean sample mean
in tail of distribution in middle of distribution
test statistic extreme test statistic not extreme
evidence to reject H0 fail to reject H0
hypothesized value hypothesized value
outside (100-α)% CI inside (100-α)% CI
test is significant at α% test is not significant at α%

4.3.6 Errors in Hypothesis Tests

  • •

    We can make two kinds of errors in hypothesis testing:

    H0 true H0 false
    Fail to reject H0 Correct decision Type II error
    Reject H0 Type I error Correct decision

Note

Type I and type II errors are similar to false positive and false negative, which we’ve discussed in earlier lectures when talking about disease testing using Bayes Theorem.

Definition: Significance and Power of a test

  • •

    All hypothesis tests have two related properties. The first is:

    • Significance level α=P⁢(type I error)=P⁢(Reject⁢H0|H0⁢true)

  • •

    Low significance is desirable.

  • •

    Just as we expect about 1 in every 20 of a set of independently constructed 95% confidence intervals not to contain μ, so too do we expect to mistakenly reject H0 for about 1 in every 20 hypothesis tests at the 5% level, given that H0 was actually true.

  • •

    For example, the number of type I errors in n independent experiments where we carry out a hypothesis test at a 10% level of significance is distributed Bin⁢(n,0.1), again, given that H0 was actually true in each case.

  • •

    The second property is:

    • Power of the test = 1−P⁢(type II error)= 1−P⁢(Fail to Reject⁢H0|H0⁢false)

    although note that this probability can’t be calculated exactly in our current setup as we don’t fix a particular value of θ in the alternative case (discussed further below).

  • •

    High power is desirable.

  • •

    The Significance and Power are similar to false positives and false negatives we saw when doing disease testing (with the order dependent on whether we identify H0 with having or not having the disease).

Discussion: Which errors are more important?

  • •

    In some situations, errors of one kind are much more important than errors of the other kind.

  • •

    For example, in testing for side effects of a drug, suppose that the null hypothesis is that there are no side effects.

  • •

    A type II error, where we mistakenly accept that there are no side effects when there truly are, is much more serious than a type I error in this case.

  • •

    By making a type I error, we mistakenly conclude that there are side effects when in fact there are none.

  • •

    A type II error could cost lives; a type I error results in lost profits.

  • •

    Aim: to design tests to have high power and low significance level

  • •

    Note that the probability of a type II error depends on tying down the alternative hypothesis, e.g. is it a one or two-sided test (as for the hypothesis tests above). In addition, we could also construct alternative hypotheses of the form:

    H0:

    μ=1.4mg

    Ha:

    μ=1.5mg

    This is an area which we won’t pursue right now.

4.3.7 Dangers of Significance Tests

  • •

    All of the dangers we considered for confidence intervals carry over to hypothesis testing, and there are a few more:

    • –

      Why should we fail to reject a hypothesis at 5.01% and yet reject at 5%? — the significance levels dichotomise the test procedure arbitrarily, when in fact the degree of support for a hypothesis has hardly changed.

      — we should use p-values rather than fixed significance levels!

    • –

      Insignificantly small effects will be detected as statistically significant if n is big enough. In other words, rejecting H0:θ=r is evidence that θ is not equal to r precisely, but says nothing about what θ might be, even θ=r+ϵ,ϵ→0.

    • –

      Assumptions (independence, normality) are sometimes difficult to check.

    • –

      If you do lots of significance tests, you will find some significant results just by chance alone — these often will not reappear when the experiment is repeated— do not perform a hypothesis test on the same data that suggested a hypothesis!

  • •

    Always first explore the data before inference.

Warning: Dangers of not examining the data

Do not apply hypothesis tests (or any other statistical inference procedure) without exploring the data first. For example, suppose we observe 50 values of a certain random variable with mean μ and unknown variance σ2, and calculate x¯=20, s=134.4. A 95% CI for μ is given by (using large n and Normal approximation):

20±(1.96)⁢(134.4)/50=20±37.2=(−17.2,57.2).

For example, the hypothesis that μ=−16 is not rejected at the 5% level. Suppose we now return to the actual observations, and they turn out to be 951 and 49 values of 1. The confidence interval that we calculated is almost certainly nonsense.

4.3.8 Are Hypothesis Tests Meaningful?

Prosecutor’s Fallacy

Remember the Prosecutor’s falacy that we encountered in Section 2.4.2, with E representing evidence and G representing guilt of the suspect:

  • •

    Recall that some of the fallacies amounted to concluding that the suspect is guilty because P⁢(E|Gc) is small.

  • •

    This was wrong, and we should actually calculate P⁢(G|E).

Hypothesis Testing

But we see a similar pattern for p-values and hypothesis tests:

  • •

    We reject H0 if p-value is small

    p-value=P( sample mean is at least as
    extreme as the one observed|H0 is true)
  • •

    However, many people interpret it as what we should calculate (if we could), which is:

    P⁢(H0⁢ is true|sample mean) (69)

    which is not the same thing.

  • •

    An expression such as is seen in equation (69) is not really available to us if we stay in the Frequentist Paradigm.

  • •

    However, the Bayesian Paradigm can provide such an expression, but it will ask us for more. Indeed, we can use Bayes theorem to rewrite equation (69) in a form which is easier to use. We will move onto this topic soon.

  • •

    Note the other strange feature of a p-value: like the Confidence Intervals, it is a probability over all the sampling experiments that we could have done, and whether they are more extreme given H0 is true. This is useful, but may not quite be what we are looking for. Again, the Bayesian Paradigm may help.

4.4 Inference for a Proportion

4.4.1 Normal Approximation

We have already looked at probabilities for proportions in Section 3. To recap the situation:

  • •

    Consider a binomially distributed random variable X with parameters n and p

    X∼Bin⁢(n,p)
  • •

    The population proportion p is unknown, and is to be estimated from data.

  • •

    The sample proportion p^=Y=X/n can be used as an estimator for p. For example, if we take a simple random sample of 1000 adults and find that the number of men is 483, our estimate of the proportion of men in the UK adult population would be y=483/1000=0.483.

  • •

    (We will mainly use Y notation here for the sample proportion, instead of p^, as it allows us to represent the observed sample proportion as y.)

  • •

    E⁢[Y]=p

  • •

    Var⁢[Y]=p⁢(1−p)n

  • •

    So that means,

    • –

      the estimator Y is unbiased,

    • –

      the variance of the estimator gets smaller as n increases.

Issue 1

  • •

    p is unknown, so Var⁢[Y] is also unknown (although can be bounded: Var⁢[Y]<14⁢n).

  • •

    Since n is large, y⁢(1−y)n should be a very good approximation for Var⁢[Y] (see Section 3.3). Here, y is the observed sample proportion.

Issue 2

  • •

    The sampling distribution of Y is hard to calculate.

  • •

    If n⁢p≥10 and n⁢(1−p)≥10 then the normal approximation is valid

So, with these two issues solved, we write:

Y∼N⁢(p,Var⁢[Y]), or equivalently ⁢Y−pVar⁢[Y]∼N⁢(0,1), with Var⁢[Y]≃y⁢(1−y)n.
  • •

    We have already developed a methodology for making inferences about population parameters given an estimate and its sampling distribution.

  • •

    Given the sampling distribution for Y, and the observed proportion y we can do hypothesis testing and construct CIs for p.

  • •

    The 1−α confidence interval for p is:

    y±z∗⁢y⁢(1−y)n

    with z∗ such that P⁢(−z∗≤Z≤z∗)=1−α for Z∼N⁢(0,1)

  • •

    The p-value for the hypothesis test H0:p=p0 vs Ha:p≠p0 is given by:

    p⁢-value=  2⁢[1−P⁢(Z<|y−p0|y⁢(1−y)n)],withZ∼N⁢(0,1)

Proof: p-value for proportions

p-value for proportions =Probability Y is as extreme as y, given H0:p=p0 is true
=P(Y≤p0−δ)+P(Y≥p0+δ))(with δ=|y−p0|)
=  2⁢P⁢(Y≥p0+δ)⁢ (by sym. of approximating Norm. dist.)
=  2⁢P⁢(Y−p0y⁢(1−y)n≥δy⁢(1−y)n)
=  2⁢P⁢(Z≥δy⁢(1−y)n)
=  2⁢[1−P⁢(Z≤δy⁢(1−y)n)]
=  2⁢[1−P⁢(Z≤|y−p0|y⁢(1−y)n)](replacing ⁢δ=|y−p0|)

4.4.2 Better Approximations

  • •

    It has been shown that the 1−α confidence interval given above is not that reliable.  In the long run, generally, it contains the population parameter p at a rate far less than 1−α.

  • •

    This is a result of the normal approximation being a poor approximation – particularly for extreme values of p and low n.

  • •

    More detailed calculations yield improved confidence intervals for p. For example:

The Wilson Interval

y+t/21+t±y⁢(1−y)⁢t+t2/41+t, with ⁢t=(z∗)2n

The Agresti-Coull Interval

y~±z∗⁢y~⁢(1−y~)n~⁢ with ⁢y~=n⁢y+2n+4⁢ and ⁢n~=n+4

4.4.3 Examples of CI’s and p-values for proportions

Example: Drop out rate, Confidence Interval

The government is very concerned about drop out rates in universities. Suppose that to estimate the first-year drop out rate p across the country, they take a simple random sample of size 250 beginning undergraduates and discover that 28 failed to continue beyond the first year.

  • •

    Calculate a standard 95% confidence interval for p, and the Wilson 95% confidence interval.

  • •

    We have that y=x/n=28/250=0.112, so that a
    standard 95% CI =

    y±z∗⁢y⁢(1−y)n =0.112±1.96⁢0.112×0.888250=[0.073,0.151]

    ⟹ 7.3% to 15.1%.

  • •

    Now try the Wilson Interval. For this we need: t=(z∗)2/n=0.0154, and then we will have:

    Wilson 95% CI =y+t/21+t±y⁢(1−y)⁢t+t2/41+t
    =0.112+0.0154/21.0154±0.112×0.888×0.0154+0.01542/41.0154
    =[0.079,0.157]

Example: Drop out rate, p-value

  • •

    Let H0:p=0.15 and Ha:p≠0.15. Calculate the p-value of this test (using the standard confidence interval).

  • •

    First we note that 0.15 is just at the edge of our 95% confidence interval so we expect the p value to be around 5%.

    p⁢-value =2⁢(1−P⁢(Z≤|y−p0|y⁢(1−y)n))
    =2⁢(1−P⁢(Z≤|0.112−0.15|0.112×0.888250))
    =2⁢(1−P⁢(Z≤1.905))=2⁢(1−0.9716)=0.0568

    hence we fail to reject H0 at the 5% level (as 0.0568>0.05)
    (this is also confirmed by the 95% confidence interval!)

Example: Psychology Experiment

An experiment was conducted to explore the effects of rotation (of characters) on recognition. A sample of 34 psychology students were recruited. Of these, 6 were men and 28 were women.

Question:

  • •

    Construct a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of psychology students which are men.

  • •

    Is this distribution representative of the UK distribution? (Recent estimates of the UK distribution of people is approximately 32.9 million men, 33.75 million women.)

Solution:

  • •

    First we assume a large population of psychology students from which these students form a sample. The proportion of men among the large population =p

  • •

    For our sample y=x/n=6/34=0.176

  • •

    95% CI for p =

    y±z∗⁢y⁢(1−y)n=0.176±1.96⁢0.176×0.82434=[0.049,0.303]⁢ or 4.9% to 30.3%
  • •

    Is this representative of the UK population?

  • •

    Let us test H0:p=32.9/(32.9+33.75)=0.493, Ha:p≠0.493

  • •

    0.493 clearly outside of 95% CI so strong evidence that psychology students are not representative of UK population (note, the Wilson 95% interval gives [0.083,0.335]).

  • •

    It will be noted that this example makes no reference to the non-binary population of psychology students. Whilst this may of interest, there are no non-binary students in the sample, hence it is reasonable to proceed in this case as though the population includes only men and women as a mathematical convenience, and consider p as being the proportion of men among those who identify as a man or a woman (as we did above). We highlight this here as Statistics is often used to make real-life inferences, and much real-world data involves sensitive topics.
